item.title: A Future for Europe’s Youth
item.dc:creator: Ana Palacio
item.description: The current generation of young Europeans possesses freedoms, material resources, opportunities to travel, and technological capabilities beyond anything previous generations could have imagined. Their demands, however, are strikingly simple: decent schools, secure jobs, affordable homes, and the possibility of raising a family.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Lou Benoist/AFP via Getty Images

The current generation of young Europeans possesses freedoms, material resources, opportunities to travel, and technological capabilities beyond anything previous generations could have imagined. Their demands, however, are strikingly simple: decent schools, secure jobs, affordable homes, and the possibility of raising a family.

By Ana Palacio

MADRID—At first glance, the wave of student-led protests that has swept across France might resemble the events of May 1968. Both featured surging crowds of demonstrators calling for education reform, criticizing the government, erecting blockades, and being confronted by riot police. Both also attracted casseurs, who turn protest into destruction. But whereas the students of 1968 were seeking to overturn the established order, today’s protesters want the established order to deliver for them.

item.title: A Tale of Two Chinas
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Rogoff
item.description: China’s economy is deeply unbalanced, with a battered real-estate sector, weak consumption, and stark regional disparities coexisting with dynamic tech and export sectors. But provided that political stability is maintained, China could continue to be a global powerhouse even as hundreds of millions of its citizens remain poor.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: CN-STR/AFP via Getty Images

China’s economy is deeply unbalanced, with a battered real-estate sector, weak consumption, and stark regional disparities coexisting with dynamic tech and export sectors. But provided that political stability is maintained, China could continue to be a global powerhouse even as hundreds of millions of its citizens remain poor.

By Kenneth Rogoff

CAMBRIDGE—Is China booming or stagnating? On one hand, its export industries—including electric vehicles, solar panels, and virtually the entire range of manufactured goods—are the envy of the world, and its tech and AI industries are second only to the United States, with Europe trailing far behind. On the other hand, as I have written many times, China is now in the sixth year of a full-blown, Japan-style real-estate crisis. Could China be booming and stagnating at the same time?

item.title: Sino–American Stability?
item.dc:creator: Stephen S. Roach
item.description: Delegates at the Bund Summit in Shanghai largely agreed that the US-China relationship could be entering a new, less contentious chapter, although many were more interested in what the post-Trump era will mean for Sino-American ties. But perhaps the most heartening sign for the future was the honest exchange of views.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Alex Wong/Getty Images

Delegates at the Bund Summit in Shanghai largely agreed that the US-China relationship could be entering a new, less contentious chapter, although many were more interested in what the post-Trump era will mean for Sino-American ties. But perhaps the most heartening sign for the future was the honest exchange of views.

By Stephen S. Roach

SHANGHAI—My search for truth inside China has been stymied. Banned from the China Development Forum (CDF), after participating for 25 years as the longest-attending foreign delegate, I feel like an outsider in what was once the country’s most prestigious international gathering. Deteriorating relations with former friends in Hong Kong, some of whom avoid eye contact with me now, have not helped matters. In both cases, I was cut off after offering constructive criticism—highlighting structural malaise in the mainland economy and a loss of autonomous identity in Hong Kong—the essence of what we call debate in the West.

item.title: Europe’s Winter of Discontent
item.dc:creator: Harold James
item.description: Although it is true that European integration has always been forged through crisis, the continent’s postwar story was largely one of incremental responses to relatively manageable challenges. Today, the European Union is facing multiple, interrelated problems that challenge its very raison d’être.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Pictures from History/Universal Images Group via Getty Images

Although it is true that European integration has always been forged through crisis, the continent’s postwar story was largely one of incremental responses to relatively manageable challenges. Today, the European Union is facing multiple, interrelated problems that challenge its very raison d’être.

By Harold James

PRINCETON—The postwar architects of European integration notoriously relied on crisis conditions to build more extensive institutions. By contrast, for incremental, piecemeal reforms to succeed, the challenges Europe faces must be relatively small. That hardly describes Europe’s current predicament.

item.title: How Students Dethroned Serbia’s Strongman
item.dc:creator: Filip Milačić
item.description: Following the ouster of Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán after 16 years in power earlier this year, the world has once again witnessed the merits of “old-school” campaigning. In toppling their own country's strongman, Serbia's new student-led opposition offers important lessons for those defending democracy elsewhere.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Andrej Isakovic/AFP via Getty Images

Following the ouster of Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán after 16 years in power earlier this year, the world has once again witnessed the merits of “old-school” campaigning. In toppling their own country's strongman, Serbia's new student-led opposition offers important lessons for those defending democracy elsewhere.

By Filip Milačić

VIENNA—After 14 years of authoritarian rule, Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have been ousted from power. Although polls had predicted a close election, the student-led opposition ultimately won by a wide margin. In an election that was neither free nor fair—owing to media capture, violence against the government’s opponents, and the SNS’s blatant misuse of state resources—the Student List won 53% of the popular vote, which translated into 141 parliamentary seats and an absolute majority. Vučić and his SNS trailed badly, with 38.8% and 103 seats.

item.title: What a US-China AI Safety Channel Needs
item.dc:creator: Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin
item.description: Addressing AI safety risks depends on close collaboration between the two leading AI powers, and the establishment of an incident-reporting channel is just a small step in this direction. But success will require that the US and Chinese governments actually understand what is happening under their own noses.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Li Zhipeng/Xinhua via Getty Images

Addressing AI safety risks depends on close collaboration between the two leading AI powers, and the establishment of an incident-reporting channel is just a small step in this direction. But success will require that the US and Chinese governments actually understand what is happening under their own noses.

By Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin

WASHINGTON, DC—The most concrete outcome from last month’s summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was an apparent agreement to set up a US-China AI incident-reporting channel. But even if either government proves willing to use this direct line or start sending data across the Pacific, they must first address a more pressing issue: US and Chinese frontier AI companies currently do not provide the information they would need.

item.title: The Authoritarian Logic of Selective Privacy
item.dc:creator: Danielle Keats Citron and Ari Waldman
item.description: Around the world, governments are increasingly deciding who gets privacy and who is denied it, a double standard that turns a fundamental democratic right into a privilege. US President Donald Trump’s administration is a prime example, shielding ICE agents from scrutiny while expanding surveillance of immigrants and protesters.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Adam Gray/Getty Images

Around the world, governments are increasingly deciding who gets privacy and who is denied it, a double standard that turns a fundamental democratic right into a privilege. US President Donald Trump’s administration is a prime example, shielding ICE agents from scrutiny while expanding surveillance of immigrants and protesters.

By Danielle Keats Citron and Ari Waldman

CHARLOTTESVILLE/IRVINE—Around the world, civil rights and civil liberties are coming under profound threat, and that threat has a name: selective privacy. The powerful enjoy it, while vulnerable groups, protesters, and others who stand up to power do not. The slogan writes itself: “Privacy for me, but not for thee.”

item.title: Brazil’s Chapter in the Anti-Authoritarian Playbook
item.dc:creator: Robert Muggah and Ilona Szabó de Carvalho
item.description: Brazil’s renewed democratic confidence must now be matched by institutional and structural reforms and a willingness to build coalitions beyond the left. Recent democratic outcomes in Hungary and Serbia offer useful lessons.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP via Getty Images

Brazil’s renewed democratic confidence must now be matched by institutional and structural reforms and a willingness to build coalitions beyond the left. Recent democratic outcomes in Hungary and Serbia offer useful lessons.

By Robert Muggah and Ilona Szabó de Carvalho

SÃO PAOLO—Until President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva staged a remarkable comeback to win re-election, no Brazilian presidential candidate had overturned a first-round defeat in a runoff. Lula did so with nearly 52% of the vote, against Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48%. More than 128 million Brazilians turned out—nearly three million more than in the first round.

item.title: Another Crash Landing for Brazil’s Economy?
item.dc:creator: Gene Frieda
item.description: Brazil’s floating exchange rate, high foreign-exchange reserves, strong commodity exports, and debt denominated predominantly in its own currency reduce its exposure to a balance-of-payments crisis. Nonetheless, continued fiscal deterioration under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will carry high domestic costs.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Rafael Martins/AFP via Getty Images

Brazil’s floating exchange rate, high foreign-exchange reserves, strong commodity exports, and debt denominated predominantly in its own currency reduce its exposure to a balance-of-payments crisis. Nonetheless, continued fiscal deterioration under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will carry high domestic costs.

By Gene Frieda

LONDON—Brazil has an unfortunate habit of disappointing. Despite the country’s exceptional natural-resource endowment, its growth trajectory resembles what Brazilians call the flight of a chicken (voo de galinha): a brief flutter followed by an inevitable fall back down to Earth. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise re-election raises the risk of another letdown.

item.title: Europe’s Make-or-Break Moment Has Arrived
item.dc:creator: Joschka Fischer
item.description: US President Donald Trump has not only abandoned Ukraine and America’s European allies, but has increasingly sided with Russian President Vladimir Putin. To preserve their sovereignty, Europeans must remain united in the face of outside pressure, which in turn requires managing political threats from within their borders.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Sean Gallup/Getty Images

US President Donald Trump has not only abandoned Ukraine and America’s European allies, but has increasingly sided with Russian President Vladimir Putin. To preserve their sovereignty, Europeans must remain united in the face of outside pressure, which in turn requires managing political threats from within their borders.

By Joschka Fischer

BERLIN—On February 24, 2027, it will have been five years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in flagrant violation of international law. Russian President Vladimir Putin’s neo-imperialist adventure—his “special military operation”—was supposed to be a brief and decisive war of conquest. But it soon became apparent that he had underestimated his victim. The Ukrainians have been determined to defend themselves, whatever it takes, and for a while, they could count on a united West, with the United States and Europe standing together in providing military and civilian support.

Continues on Project Syndicate (registration required)

item.title: Middle Powers Can Lead on AI Safety
item.dc:creator: Gordon LaForge and Robert C. Orr
item.description: With the United States showing no interest in regulating AI, middle powers have an opportunity to take the lead on governance. By banding together, these countries could condition market access on meeting a common set of safety requirements and explore joint investment in technical capacity.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images

With the United States showing no interest in regulating AI, middle powers have an opportunity to take the lead on governance. By banding together, these countries could condition market access on meeting a common set of safety requirements and explore joint investment in technical capacity.

By Gordon LaForge and Robert C. Orr

WASHINGTON, DC—The warnings about the safety of frontier AI models continue to grow louder. Writing in Time in early October, the former chief scientist of the United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute put the probability of us all dying because of smarter-than-human AI systems at 50%. On the same day, a senior OpenAI employee announced that he had left the company because of its “broken” safety culture. But the United States has shown no interest in regulating the technology, except for a “morally binding” voluntary accord recently signed by tech CEOs and US President Donald Trump.

Continues on Project Syndicate (registration required)

item.title: Lula Killed the Donroe Doctrine
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Adelman
item.description: In attempting to disentangle the United States from the rest of the world and retreat into a seemingly controllable hemispheric stronghold, Donald Trump's Latin America strategy had fared better than the rest of his foreign policy. But following a defeat for the far right in Brazil, his project now looks dead in the water.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Alexandre Schneider/Getty Images

In attempting to disentangle the United States from the rest of the world and retreat into a seemingly controllable hemispheric stronghold, Donald Trump's Latin America strategy had fared better than the rest of his foreign policy. But following a defeat for the far right in Brazil, his project now looks dead in the water.

By Jeremy Adelman

RIO DE JANEIRO—Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory in Brazil’s presidential election is a blow to Donald Trump’s plan for the Western Hemisphere. The US president was hoping to huddle with client states to the south who mimic his business and mano dura (iron fist) posturing, while further betraying liberal partners. That plan, within reach until Sunday’s vote, is now in tatters.

item.title: The Wrong Way to Compare Economic Size
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Frankel
item.description: At the European Central Bank’s annual research conference, Paul Krugman concluded that, when it comes to “weaponized interdependence,” the EU is more powerful than both the US and China. But his reliance on PPP-adjusted GDP as a way to smooth out the volatility of nominal exchange rates ignores the even greater swings in PPP data.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Ng Han Guan/Pool/AFP via Getty Images

At the European Central Bank’s annual research conference, Paul Krugman concluded that, when it comes to “weaponized interdependence,” the EU is more powerful than both the US and China. But his reliance on PPP-adjusted GDP as a way to smooth out the volatility of nominal exchange rates ignores the even greater swings in PPP data.

By Jeffrey Frankel

CAMBRIDGE—Last month, the Nobel laureate economist Paul Krugman gave a talk at the European Central Bank’s annual research conference, which focused on geoeconomics. The term refers to countries’ ability to exploit economic interactions for geopolitical ends. Think of China’s threats to cut off trading partners from its exports of rare-earth minerals.

item.title: Public Control for a Purposeful Economy
item.dc:creator: Mariana Mazzucato and Anna Hope Emerson
item.description: As more governments recognize the need for greater public control over economic outcomes, they must be careful to define the concept well. What ultimately matters is not ownership, but the state’s capacity to steer economic activity toward strategic objectives in the service of the common good.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Stefan Rousseau/WPA/Pool/Getty Images

As more governments recognize the need for greater public control over economic outcomes, they must be careful to define the concept well. What ultimately matters is not ownership, but the state’s capacity to steer economic activity toward strategic objectives in the service of the common good.

By Mariana Mazzucato and Anna Hope Emerson

LONDON—Governments around the world say they have no room to act. Although inequality and the cost of living are rising, fiscal space, we are told, is tight. Yet in many cases, the squeeze is self-imposed. It follows from equating fiscal responsibility with cutting deficits and debt, rather than with building an economy’s capacity to grow, withstand shocks, and meet its obligations over time. In fact, cutting spending in a weak economy can leave the debt-to-GDP ratio higher, not lower; and when fiscal rules bite, public investment is often the first thing cut.

item.title: Rethinking Sustainable Livelihoods From the Ground Up
item.dc:creator: Grita Anindarini
item.description: In regions where economic activity has long revolved around fossil-fuel extraction, ensuring a just transition requires developing alternative livelihoods that account for each community’s specific needs. Regional endowment funds could be a useful vehicle for funding these local initiatives.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Chaideer Mahyuddin/AFP via Getty Images

In regions where economic activity has long revolved around fossil-fuel extraction, ensuring a just transition requires developing alternative livelihoods that account for each community’s specific needs. Regional endowment funds could be a useful vehicle for funding these local initiatives.

By Grita Anindarini

JAKARTA—When the energy transition confronts difficult economic conditions within a country, addressing the transition’s unequal impact becomes both more challenging and more imperative. In Indonesia, with an economy recently described as a “ticking time bomb,” coal mining has long been the main driver of GDP in certain regencies and provinces. Pursuit of the energy transition in such places raises the tricky political question of how to support economic diversification, and boost economic growth, in these areas while also combating climate change.

The answer may seem obvious: reducing vulnerability to economic shocks caused by the shift away from fossil fuels requires broadening income sources. But that is easier said than done. A just energy transition requires a wider transformation that includes creating meaningful job opportunities, closing human-capital gaps, and alleviating poverty. Most importantly, these efforts must be highly localized to account for each area’s unique strengths and each community’s specific needs.

Pulau Panggung, a village located in Muara Enim, one of Indonesia’s most coal-dependent regencies, in South Sumatra province, illustrates this vulnerability starkly. According to research by WALHI Sumatera Selatan (Friends of the Earth South Sumatera) and the Indonesian Center for Environmental Law, 56.7% of the village’s residents are employed as mine workers, including casual laborers. When coal mining arrived in the early 1990s, the community largely abandoned farming, its main economic engine at the time. Now, as mining firms face expiring contracts and begin implementing efficiency measures, villagers’ livelihoods are under threat, but this time without a ready-made substitute.

The village’s post-coal economy could return to agriculture and embrace nature-based tourism. But shifting to these sectors requires a healthy ecosystem, making it essential to force companies to fulfill their obligations to restore mined land. Moreover, because villagers gave up farming decades ago, they would need training in sustainable agriculture techniques and opportunities to develop skills for other alternative livelihoods, such as digital-based marketing.

Some of the barriers to creating new livelihoods in Pulau Panggung are structural, such as the ambiguous legal status of land, a long-standing problem across Indonesia. But the bigger challenge, both here and elsewhere, is the lack of formal channels for developing effective local initiatives. Each village’s strengths must serve as the foundation for community-based economic transformation. Unfortunately, Indonesia’s top-down policymaking and regulatory regime, particularly in the energy sector, hinders efforts to maximize local strengths.

The Indonesian government directs transition planning by providing general guidance, which provincial and regency plans should theoretically elaborate on, identifying what is unique to each place. Yet the 2025–2029 South Sumatra medium-term regional development plan gives no clear direction on how economic transformation will be carried out, only that efforts to move away from a coal-based economy remain suboptimal. The plan recognizes that natural resources must play a role but does not explain how to use them in a way that fits the needs of each village and avoids harming ecosystems.

This problem is not unique to Indonesia. Many other governments have similar gaps in their energy-transition policies. The key is for policymakers to enable a more bottom-up approach by focusing on two objectives.

First, policymakers must directly involve affected communities. Entrusting transition planning to local governments and giving communities a genuine role in the decision-making process would help officials and companies design tailored interventions that expand employment opportunities for workers at risk of displacement.

Embedding community-driven initiatives in these policies must begin with local assessments. Before any plan is approved, the government should conduct participatory mapping of livelihoods, land status, workforce skills, and local strengths. In Pulau Panggung, this kind of mapping would highlight its agricultural and tourism potential.

Second, policymakers should explore the possibility of a regional fund that could redirect government revenue derived from mining and fossil-fuel production toward supporting community-based transitions. One model to follow is the Alaska Permanent Fund, whereby the state government invests a portion of its oil and mining revenues for the long-term benefit of all current and future Alaskans.

Managed by a state-owned corporation, this sovereign wealth fund helps finance public services like education, health care, and basic infrastructure. Policymakers, in both developed and developing countries alike, can use such a vehicle to ensure a sustainable economic transition by operating transparently and allowing local communities to direct the proceeds toward their chosen priorities.

Time is running out to establish regional endowment funds. Policymakers in Indonesia and other countries must act before mining and fossil-fuel revenues stop flowing. As a first step, they can run pilots in affected regions—like Muara Enim—to show what is possible. Waiting too long risks leaving these communities with a plan but no capital to implement it.

Grita Anindarini is a senior strategist at the Indonesian Center for Environmental Law.

Originally published on Project Syndicate

item.title: The Specter of an AI-Driven Slowdown
item.dc:creator: Dambisa Moyo
item.description: The rush to finance AI infrastructure is driving up borrowing costs just as governments grapple with mounting debt and persistent fiscal deficits. If the AI investment boom falters, falling valuations could choke off financing, with little room for fiscal and monetary policy to cushion the economic shock.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Myung J. Chun/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

The rush to finance AI infrastructure is driving up borrowing costs just as governments grapple with mounting debt and persistent fiscal deficits. If the AI investment boom falters, falling valuations could choke off financing, with little room for fiscal and monetary policy to cushion the economic shock.

By Dambisa Moyo

ISTANBUL—Today’s economic growth depends heavily on AI investment and fiscal spending. The International Monetary Fund estimates that AI could add up to half a percentage point to annual global growth over the next decade, raising the average rate from 3% to 3.5%.

item.title: Is a Chinese Implosion Looming?
item.dc:creator: Navneeraj Sharma and Arvind Subramanian
item.description: If current trends continue, the Chinese state will find itself exposed to a political succession crisis, a weakening economy, and a lack of resources to exercise power domestically and project it externally. It would be a perfect storm, with far-reaching global repercussions.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Simon Song/South China Morning Post via Getty Images

If current trends continue, the Chinese state will find itself exposed to a political succession crisis, a weakening economy, and a lack of resources to exercise power domestically and project it externally. It would be a perfect storm, with far-reaching global repercussions.

By Navneeraj Sharma and Arvind Subramanian

NEW DELHI—This has been an era of shocks. In the space of two decades, the world has witnessed globally disruptive wars—from Iraq in the 2000s to Ukraine and Iran today—a global financial crisis, a global pandemic, and a rogue American president upending the global order. Now, yet another potential shock must be addressed: Though few dare to speculate about it publicly, an economic and political perfect storm is bearing down on China.

Continues on Project Syndicate (registration required)

item.title: PS Events: Reinventing Europe – Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
item.dc:creator: PS editors
item.description: When we talk about "reinvention" we often overlook what works, noted WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala in her closing keynote. This is true of the global trading system, which has proven surprisingly resilient in recent years, and of the European economy, which might not have a tech giant to rival those in the US or China, but remains a global trade powerhouse and a leader in science and research. While Europe has much to do to improve its external competitiveness, it must not act from a sense of panic. Instead, it must pursue measured reforms and seize new opportunities, not least closer trade and investment ties with Africa.

item.title: Who Pays the Fiscal Watchdogs?
item.dc:creator: Janet Zhou
item.description: Civil-society oversight is the cheapest insurance in sovereign finance, because it enables independent scrutiny long before a default. But given that a borrowing government will never volunteer to fund the people who audit it, global decision-makers must do so using agreements for stolen-asset recovery and sovereign-debt treatments.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: z_wei/Getty Images

Civil-society oversight is the cheapest insurance in sovereign finance, because it enables independent scrutiny long before a default. But given that a borrowing government will never volunteer to fund the people who audit it, global decision-makers must do so using agreements for stolen-asset recovery and sovereign-debt treatments.

By Janet Zhou

HARARE—In 2021, Zimbabwean Finance Minister Mthuli Ncube caused an uproar when he issued more than $15 million in guarantees for private loans made by the Commercial Bank of Zimbabwe without seeking parliament’s approval. It was a particularly flagrant example of an unfortunately common practice in Zimbabwe: committing state resources to non-essential projects that offer no public benefit. Some of these loans invariably went unpaid, leaving taxpayers to cover the losses.

In April 2022, the Zimbabwe Coalition on Debt and Development (which I led at the time), together with three co-applicants, petitioned the High Court of Zimbabwe to declare that parliament must approve public borrowing before it happens. In March 2023, the Court ordered the government to gazette a bill in the next 12 months outlining parliament’s role in approving loans and guarantees and establishing the procedure for ratification or rejection.

This win was possible only because of a grant. The Open Society Initiative for Southern Africa, a regional foundation, funded the external lawyers who argued it, as well as our researchers, on a three-year cycle. When the cycle ended, the capacity to fight these legal battles went with it.

This model of financing public accountability in developing countries through grants has started to collapse. Aid from OECD donors fell by 23.1% in real terms in 2025, the largest annual drop ever recorded. Meanwhile, governments are tightening the requirements for registering civil-society organizations and limiting which of these groups can receive funding from abroad. Zimbabwe’s Private Voluntary Organisations Amendment Act, enacted in April 2025, allows the authorities to cancel the registration of civil-society organizations and seize their assets without judicial oversight. El Salvador’s Foreign Agents Law, passed just one month later, imposed a 30% tax on all foreign funding.

The weakening of civil-society participation will be felt widely, not least because every proposal for making global finance more sustainable and equitable depends on citizens who can read a debt-sustainability analysis and force a minister to answer for it. The Sevilla Commitment, adopted at last year’s Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, calls for strengthening parliamentary oversight of debt, independent audit institutions, and civil society’s role in exposing illicit financial flows. But nobody has said who pays for that work.

The answer may lie in two types of international instruments: agreements for stolen-asset recovery and sovereign-debt treatments. Each could contain a clause mandating that a fixed share of the sum—5% is a justifiable starting point—goes toward funding independent oversight of public finance in the recipient country. The money would be protected from executive interference, publicly audited, and guaranteed for the life of the program.

This has already been done in agreements for asset returns. In December 2017, Switzerland repatriated roughly $321 million stolen by former Nigerian President Sani Abacha under an agreement that provided for World Bank monitoring and civil-society oversight of how the money was spent. That same year, the United Kingdom, the United States, and four focus countries—Nigeria, Sri Lanka, Tunisia, and Ukraine—adopted the GFAR (Global Forum on Asset Recovery) principles, which commit governments that are returning or receiving assets to transparency and accountability.

But, to date, such monitoring has been treated as a courtesy, extended at the discretion of the government that happens to be holding the stolen funds. The Sevilla Commitment calls for piloting new approaches to asset return, including a clause in these agreements stipulating that a third party monitors the disbursement of money for oversight to prevent tampering from the recipient government.

Debt treatments, negotiated in creditor committees and multilateral fora, could adopt a similar approach: channel a fixed share of debt-service savings to an independently governed fund that supports public-finance oversight. Grants would be awarded competitively, published in a database, and externally audited against criteria written into the settlement.

Creditors have already accepted similar terms for different categories. In 1998, Uganda ring-fenced its debt-relief savings under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries Initiative, earmarking them for anti-poverty programs. In 2023, Ecuador completed a debt-for-nature swap in which part of the interest on the new loan pays roughly $12 million annually, for 18.5 years, into a fund for maintaining the Galápagos Islands, governed by a board of representatives from government, academia, and business.

A borrowing government will never volunteer to fund the people who audit it. But when the obligation is written into these settlements, the money survives the next budget or election. It also gives creditors insight into the borrower’s disclosure practices.

Oversight is the cheapest insurance in sovereign finance. A group of economists tracking revelations of undisclosed debt across 154 countries over the past century found that nearly half of all sovereign defaults coincided with substantial upward revisions to reported public debt. Hidden debt piles up in good times and surfaces in bad times, when someone finally examines the books. If public oversight is properly funded, outside scrutiny begins long before a default and can pave the way for reform.

Consider the order that we won from Zimbabwe’s High Court. It was an important outcome that nonetheless failed to dent the problem. A bill was drafted but not gazetted; the Court’s deadline passed with no action. The organizations that could have fought in the courts for its enforcement had moved on to other grant-funded work.

As efforts to revamp the global financial architecture accelerate, policymakers must recognize that improving debt management starts with accountability at home. At the International Monetary Fund-World Bank Annual Meetings in October, the new Borrowers’ Platform, which seeks to give developing countries a stronger voice in global debt discussions, held its first Governing Council. While proactive coordination between finance ministers and central-bank governors, as the officials who sign the loans, is essential to achieve sustainable debt levels, it must be coupled with long-term external funding for civil-society groups that can hold them to their word.

Janet Zhou is Executive Director of the African Forum and Network on Debt and Development (AFRODAD).

Originally published on Project Syndicate

item.title: How to Help Left-Behind Regions
item.dc:creator: Keun Lee
item.description: Pouring public investment into poorer towns and cities might be politically beneficial, but the economic returns of indiscriminate largesse would be limited. A better approach would concentrate investment in areas with the potential to become high-productivity hubs, such as large peripheral cities.
item.content:encoded:

Pouring public investment into poorer towns and cities might be politically beneficial, but the economic returns of indiscriminate largesse would be limited. A better approach would concentrate investment in areas with the potential to become high-productivity hubs, such as large peripheral cities.

By Keun Lee

SEOUL—Discussion of economic inequality usually focuses on disparities across countries or the divide between rich and poor households within them. But greater attention is now being devoted to domestic regional differences, whether between the capital city and the rest of the country (as in South Korea and the United Kingdom), between northern and southern regions (as in Italy), or between coastal cities and inland areas (as in China and the United States).
